title: An Open Recipe for IMO Gold: Training Nemotron for Olympiad Mathematics
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 9 Sep 2026]
    Title:An Open Recipe for IMO Gold: Training Nemotron for Olympiad Mathematics
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:We study how model post-training and test-time inference design affect natural-language proof generation for hard olympiad mathematics. Starting from Nemotron 3 Ultra, we train two specialist checkpoints using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, and evaluate checkpoint choice, verification, and refinement. Based on these findings, we present an open-model test-time-compute pipeline. The system operates entirely in natural language, with no formal prover, external tools, or internet access. Three Nemotron 3 Ultra checkpoints - the general-availability model and two post-trained specialists - power an iterative search that generates, verifies, and refines candidate proofs; a separate high-compute stage then selects each final submission. The system scored 30 out of 42 points at IMO 2026, reaching the gold-medal threshold. We release the two post-trained checkpoints as well as the training data, the training and inference code, the submitted solutions, and Nemotron-IMO-Bench, a new benchmark of 200 novel olympiad-level problems.

report.summary: NVIDIA researchers release an open recipe showing Nemotron 3 Ultra post-trained with SFT and RL can reach IMO 2026 gold via natural-language proof search.
report.background: AI systems have made rapid progress on mathematics, from formal theorem provers like Lean and Isabelle to neural models that solve algebra and calculus. But olympiad problems require creative, multi-step natural-language proofs, a challenge where models often hallucinate or lose logical chains. Previous strong systems frequently relied on formal verification, external tools, or internet access, limiting openness and reproducibility. Recent gains have come from post-training—supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning—plus test-time compute, where models generate many candidates and select the best. The IMO gold threshold remains a key milestone. This paper, submitted September 2026, presents an open recipe built on Nemotron 3 Ultra, aiming to show that careful post-training and inference design can deliver gold-medal performance without formal provers or external aids.
key_points: The team starts from Nemotron 3 Ultra and creates two specialist checkpoints using supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. They systematically compare checkpoint choices and study verification and refinement strategies, showing these post-training steps are central to strong olympiad proof generation rather than a single general model.

The inference pipeline combines three Nemotron 3 Ultra checkpoints: the general-availability model and two post-trained specialists. They power an iterative search that generates, verifies, and refines candidate proofs, followed by a separate high-compute stage that selects each final submission.

The system works entirely in natural language. It uses no formal prover, no external tools, and no internet access, contrasting with systems that lean on Lean, Python, or retrieval. This makes the approach simpler to reproduce but places heavy demands on model reasoning and test-time compute.

At IMO 2026, the system scored 30 out of 42 points, reaching the gold-medal threshold. This demonstrates that an open-model, natural-language test-time-compute pipeline can compete at the highest level of olympiad mathematics.

The authors release the two post-trained checkpoints, training data, training and inference code, submitted solutions, and Nemotron-IMO-Bench, a new benchmark of 200 novel olympiad-level problems. This open release supports reproducibility and lets others test generalization rather than rely on contaminated public sets.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this shifts attention from proprietary formal systems toward open post-training recipes and test-time compute as the main levers for advanced reasoning. Developers gain checkpoints, data, code, and a fresh benchmark to fine-tune, compare methods, and build math-focused agents without starting from scratch. Regular users may see better tutoring, homework help, and step-by-step explanations, though high compute costs and the risk of benchmark overfitting remain. The result also strengthens the case that natural-language reasoning can approach formal methods for olympiad tasks, potentially accelerating AI-for-math and AI-for-science. It does not eliminate verification concerns: proof correctness still needs careful human or formal checking.
report.tools: Follow NVIDIA's Nemotron model family and Hugging Face releases for the two checkpoints and data. Try the Nemotron-IMO-Bench benchmark for evaluation. Related open projects include Lean, Isabelle, and Coq for formal verification; DeepSeek-Prover and AlphaProof for neural theorem proving; Qwen-Math, OpenMathInstruct, and MATH for training and testing. arXiv HTML and GitHub links in the paper provide code and inference scripts.
